h1: Commercial Roof Insurance Appraisal: How to Resolve Roof Claim Disputes
excerpt: How a commercial roof insurance appraisal resolves hail and wind disputes: roof systems, evidence like core samples, cosmetic damage issues and Texas-specific rules.
key_takeaways: Roof appraisal resolves disputes over the amount of a covered commercial roof loss.
Core samples and moisture surveys often decide repair versus replacement.
Cosmetic damage exclusions drive many metal roof disputes in Texas.
Rooftop equipment, insulation and flashings are frequently left out of estimates.
Texas appraisers decide amount of loss, not coverage.
body_html:
A commercial roof insurance appraisal resolves disputes between a building owner and the insurer over how much a covered roof loss is worth. Each side appoints an independent appraiser to inspect the roof and price the repair or replacement, and an umpire decides anything they cannot agree on. It is usually faster and less costly than litigation.

What is a commercial roof insurance appraisal?

Most commercial property policies include an appraisal clause. When the owner and the carrier agree that a roof was damaged by a covered event, such as hail or wind, but disagree on the amount of loss, either side can demand appraisal in writing.

The appraisal process then follows the policy's terms. Each side selects a competent, disinterested appraiser. The two appraisers select an umpire. They inspect the roof, compare estimates and try to agree. Anything they cannot resolve goes to the umpire, and a written award signed by any two of the three sets the amount of loss.

A roof appraisal is not a real estate appraisal and it is not a general roof condition survey. It is focused entirely on valuing the covered damage. If you are new to the concept, start with our guide on whether appraisal can be used for roof claims.

Why commercial roof claims are so often disputed

Commercial roofs are large, expensive and technically complex. That combination creates plenty of room for honest disagreement and for underpayment. The most common sticking points are:

  • Repair versus replacement. The carrier proposes patching impact points while the owner's roofer says the membrane or panel system is compromised and needs replacement.
  • Hidden damage. Hail can fracture membranes, crush insulation board or damage the cover board beneath a surface that looks intact.
  • Wet insulation. Moisture trapped in the roof assembly may require removal and replacement of insulation, not just the top layer.
  • Recover versus tear-off. Building codes generally limit recovering over existing roofs, particularly where there are already multiple layers or wet materials, which can force a full tear-off.
  • Rooftop equipment. HVAC units, condenser fins, skylights, vents and curbs are often left out or treated as cosmetic.
  • Cosmetic damage exclusions. Many commercial policies, especially for metal roofs, exclude damage that affects appearance only. Whether dents are cosmetic or functional becomes the central fight.
  • Pricing and access. Large commercial projects involve cranes, safety requirements, phased work around tenants and specialty crews that database pricing may understate.

Common commercial roof systems and their claim issues

Each roof system fails differently and raises different questions in a claim. The table below summarizes what we see most often in Texas.

Roof systemTypical hail or wind damageCommon claim dispute
TPO and PVC single-plyMembrane fractures, seam damage, punctures, crushed insulationWhether fractures exist below the surface and whether repairs are feasible
EPDMBruising, punctures, seam separation, wind upliftWhether aged membranes can be repaired or must be replaced
Modified bitumen and built-up roofsGranule loss, mat fractures, blistering, gravel displacementDistinguishing hail fractures from age-related wear
Metal (standing seam and R-panel)Dents, seam and fastener damage, coating damageCosmetic damage exclusions versus functional damage
Spray polyurethane foam and coatingsFractured coatings, exposed foam, moisture intrusionRecoating versus foam removal and replacement

Flat and low-slope systems bring their own set of problems, which we cover in flat roof insurance claim challenges. Metal roofs deserve special attention; see our guide to the insurance estimate for metal roof damage.

How the commercial roof appraisal process works

  1. Review the policy. Confirm the appraisal clause, deductibles (often a percentage for wind and hail in Texas), any cosmetic damage exclusion, and whether the roof is on a replacement cost or actual cash value schedule.
  2. Send the written demand. Identify the claim number, date of loss and the amount in dispute.
  3. Appoint appraisers. Each side names its appraiser, commonly within about 20 days of the demand.
  4. Select an umpire. The appraisers agree on an umpire, or a court appoints one if they cannot.
  5. Inspect the roof. Appraisers walk the roof together or separately, often with test cuts, core samples and moisture surveys.
  6. Exchange estimates. Each appraiser prepares a line-item estimate covering roofing, insulation, flashings, rooftop equipment, access and code items.
  7. Resolve differences. The appraisers work through scope and pricing line by line and submit remaining disputes to the umpire.
  8. Sign the award. Two signatures make the award. The carrier then applies the deductible, prior payments and depreciation.
Tip: Ask for core samples and a moisture survey early. Physical evidence of what is under the membrane, such as crushed insulation or trapped water, is often what moves a commercial roof dispute from repair to replacement.

Evidence that strengthens a roof appraisal

Commercial roof appraisals turn on evidence. The strongest files usually include:

  • Date-of-loss weather data, such as hail reports and storm data from the National Weather Service and NOAA.
  • Close-up photos with scale, showing impact marks, fractures and seam damage, marked by roof section.
  • Core samples and test cuts documenting each layer of the assembly.
  • Moisture surveys using infrared, capacitance or similar methods, with a map of wet areas.
  • Drone and aerial imagery for overall layout and accurate measurements.
  • Maintenance and inspection records showing the roof's condition before the storm.
  • Manufacturer specifications and warranty requirements, which can affect whether repairs are acceptable.
  • Detailed line-item estimates and specialty contractor bids for items the database prices poorly.

Accurate measurements matter on large roofs because every square foot is multiplied by a unit price. Our free roof square calculator covers pitch and waste on sloped sections.

Cosmetic vs functional damage on commercial roofs

This issue drives a large share of metal roof disputes. A cosmetic damage exclusion typically removes coverage for dents or marks that affect appearance but not the roof's ability to shed water or its expected service life.

Whether a particular dent is cosmetic or functional is often a factual question about damage, which appraisers can evaluate. Signs that point toward functional damage include fractured or compromised coatings that expose metal to corrosion, deformed seams or laps that allow water entry, loosened or damaged fasteners, and damage to panels that affects drainage. Our guide to cosmetic damage in roofing claims explains the distinction in more detail.

Whether the exclusion applies at all, however, is a coverage question. Under State Farm Lloyds v. Johnson (Tex. 2009), Texas appraisers decide the amount of loss and may consider causation and the extent of damage, but not coverage. Many awards separate items so the parties can apply coverage decisions afterward. This is general information, not legal advice.

Industrial roof insurance loss evaluation

Warehouses, manufacturing plants and distribution centers often have the largest roofs in a claim portfolio, sometimes covering many acres. Industrial roof insurance loss evaluation adds challenges beyond typical commercial roofs:

  • Very large areas where small unit-price differences become large dollar differences
  • Operations, inventory and equipment that cannot easily be moved during repairs
  • Rooftop exhaust fans, process equipment and skylights in high numbers
  • Roof assemblies that were recovered once or more over the building's life
  • Safety and access requirements that raise labor costs

For these properties, an appraiser who can produce a complete, defensible estimate, rather than simply reviewing the carrier's, is especially important.

Commercial roof claims in Texas

Texas sees some of the most frequent large hail in the country, and commercial roofs across Dallas–Fort Worth, Austin, San Antonio, Amarillo, Lubbock and Midland–Odessa take repeated hits. Coastal properties in Houston and Corpus Christi face hurricane winds that peel membranes and damage flashing and edge metal.

A few Texas-specific points to remember:

  • Percentage deductibles for wind and hail are common, so the net recovery depends heavily on the total value of the building.
  • Roof payment schedules on some commercial policies limit older roofs to actual cash value or a scheduled percentage.
  • Prompt payment rules under Texas Insurance Code chapter 542 continue to apply to the claim.
  • Pre-suit notice under chapter 542A generally requires 61 days for weather claims.

Owners in North Texas can find local details on our Fort Worth insurance appraiser page, and our article on commercial roof hail damage claims goes deeper on hail specifically.

Is a commercial roof insurance appraisal worth it?

A commercial roof insurance appraisal makes the most sense when three things are true: the carrier has accepted that the roof was damaged by a covered event, there is a meaningful dollar gap between the carrier's estimate and a qualified contractor's or appraiser's estimate, and the disagreement is about scope or price rather than whether the policy applies.

For example, if a carrier pays to repair 40 impact points on a 60,000-square-foot TPO roof but core samples show fractured membrane and crushed insulation across most of the field, the gap between repair and replacement can be very large. That is the kind of dispute commercial roof appraisal is built for. The numbers here are illustrative, but the pattern is common after Texas hailstorms.

Appraisal is less useful when the carrier denies the claim entirely on coverage grounds, or when the gap is small enough that appraiser and umpire fees would consume most of the recovery. Weigh the likely difference against the cost before you send the demand, and make sure your own estimate is complete enough to defend.

Next steps for your commercial roof claim

If the carrier's estimate patches a roof your contractor says must be replaced, or leaves out insulation, flashings and rooftop equipment, an independent review can quantify the gap before you decide whether to invoke appraisal.

Choosing a commercial roof appraiser

Look for an appraiser with hands-on experience inspecting commercial roof systems, writing detailed Xactimate or Symbility estimates, and understanding core samples, moisture surveys and manufacturer requirements. Independence matters because most policies require a disinterested appraiser.

faqs.q: What is a roof appraisal in an insurance claim?
faqs.a: A roof appraisal is the policy-based process for settling a disagreement over the value of covered roof damage. Each side appoints an appraiser, the appraisers inspect and price the roof, and an umpire decides unresolved items. An award signed by two of the three sets the amount of loss under the policy.

faqs.q: How long does a commercial roof appraisal take?
faqs.a: Many commercial roof appraisals take a few months from written demand to signed award. Timing depends on how quickly appraisers and an umpire are selected, how large and complex the roof is, whether testing such as core samples is needed, and how many items remain disputed after the appraisers compare estimates.

faqs.q: Can appraisal decide if hail damage on a metal roof is cosmetic?
faqs.a: Texas appraisers can evaluate the extent and nature of damage, including whether dents affect function. Whether a cosmetic damage exclusion applies is a coverage question for the parties or a court. Awards often itemize damage so coverage decisions can be applied afterward without redoing the appraisal.

faqs.q: Who pays for a commercial roof appraisal?
faqs.a: Under most appraisal clauses, each party pays its own appraiser and the umpire fee is shared equally. Testing costs such as core samples or moisture surveys are often handled by the party requesting them. Review your policy and get your appraiser fee agreement in writing before the process begins.

faqs.q: Does a commercial roof need tear-off or can it be recovered?
faqs.a: It depends on the existing layers, the condition of the insulation and deck, the local code and manufacturer requirements. Codes generally restrict recovering over roofs with multiple layers or wet materials. Core samples and moisture surveys help determine whether a recover is allowed or a full tear-off is required.
